faq.a: LED stands for light-emitting diode. It is a diode, a one-way valve for current, made from a material that gives off light when current flows through it the right way.

faq.q: What happens inside an LED chip?
faq.a: The chip has two layers: one with spare electrons, one with gaps called holes. When current flows, electrons cross the junction and fall into the holes, giving off their extra energy as light.
asks: How do electrons make light in an LED?

faq.q: What decides the colour of an LED?
faq.a: The material sets how far each electron drops in energy. A big drop gives blue light and a smaller drop gives red. White LEDs are usually blue LEDs coated with a yellow phosphor.
asks: How do LEDs make different colours?

faq.q: Why don't LEDs get as hot as old bulbs?
faq.a: An LED makes light directly from electrons dropping in energy, not by heating a wire white-hot. Much more of the energy comes out as light, though the chip still warms a little.

faq.q: Why does an LED only work one way round?
faq.a: It is a diode, so it lets current through in only one direction. Connect it backwards and nothing flows, so it stays dark. The longer leg usually goes to the positive side.
asks: Which way round does an LED go?

facts: The 2014 Nobel Prize in Physics went to Isamu Akasaki, Hiroshi Amano and Shuji Nakamura for efficient blue LEDs.
Most white LEDs are blue LEDs coated with a yellow phosphor.
